title: Database Caching Patterns
description: Explore query caching, buffer pools, and materialized views to reduce database load and speed up reads.

data.text: Databases are often the bottleneck in read-heavy systems. Database caching reduces expensive disk I/O and computation by storing frequently accessed results closer to the query engine. This can happen inside the database itself with buffer pools, outside the database with query caches, or through precomputed structures like materialized views.

Most relational databases maintain an in-memory buffer pool or page cache that holds recently used data pages. When a query requests rows that are already in the buffer pool, the database skips disk access entirely. Tuning the buffer pool size for your workload is one of the simplest and highest-impact database performance optimizations. In PostgreSQL, shared_buffers controls this pool. In MySQL, innodb_buffer_pool_size serves the same role.

data.text: Query caching stores the result set of a query so that identical subsequent queries can be answered from memory. Some databases offer built-in query caches, while others rely on external caches like Redis. Query caches work best when the underlying data changes infrequently and the same query is executed repeatedly. They become counterproductive if the cached data becomes stale quickly or if the query workload is highly variable.

data.title: Staleness Risk
data.text: Query caches can return outdated results if the underlying tables are updated. Always validate whether your consistency requirements tolerate eventual consistency before enabling query caching at the database layer.

A materialized view stores the result of a query physically on disk, just like a regular table. Unlike a standard view, which recomputes on every access, a materialized view can be refreshed on a schedule or triggered manually. This makes materialized views ideal for expensive aggregations such as daily revenue totals, user activity dashboards, or reporting queries that do not require real-time accuracy.

data.title: Pattern Selection Exercise
data.description: You are optimizing a reporting dashboard that runs heavy aggregations on a transactional database.
steps: Choose between a materialized view, query cache, or external cache.
Explain the refresh strategy and consistency trade-offs.
data.expectedOutcome: A short recommendation with justification for the chosen database caching pattern.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Buffer pools cache data pages inside the database
Query caches store result sets for repeated queries
Choose the pattern based on data volatility and consistency requirements
data.takeaway: Database caching reduces I/O and computation, but only when the caching pattern matches the access pattern and freshness requirements.
